edges.note: The client proxy forwards each invocation to a Requestor that constructs and sends the remote request.
Requestor hands the marshaled message to a Client Request Handler to manage the connection and transmit it.
Invoker relies on the Server Request Handler as its transport, receiving request messages and returning replies through it.
Client-side Requestor and server-side Invoker are complementary halves of one remote invocation.
Peer transport handlers on the two ends of the wire cooperate to move request and reply messages.
The Broker infrastructure is built from a Requestor as its client-side invocation machinery.
The Broker dispatches incoming requests to target objects through an Invoker.
A Broker exposes remote components to clients via generated Client Proxies presenting the remote interface.
Both share one logical object across address spaces; Bodyguard guards a shared object, HOPP splits it into two active halves.
Bodyguard shares an object with a validating guard instead of full RPC forwarding done by a client proxy.
Both replicate data; single-leader routes all writes to one node, multi-leader accepts writes at several.
Two of DDIA's three replication approaches: multiple leaders vs quorum writes with no leader.
Leader-based streaming vs client/coordinator quorum writes are competing replication strategies.
Single-leader is one concrete form of the general replication pattern.
Multi-leader is one concrete form of the general replication pattern.
Leaderless/quorum is one concrete form of the general replication pattern.
A replicated component group applies replication at the component/service level for availability.
On primary failure a leader-election chooses the replica to promote as the new leader.
Instances detect a failed leader via missed heartbeats/timeout, triggering re-election.
A replica group commonly elects one coordinator to sequence updates or own a role.

edges.cite: Kleppmann, DDIA ch.6 (partitioning and replication combined)
edges.note: Partitioning and replication are normally combined: each shard is also replicated for availability.
Sharding gives each shared-nothing node exclusive ownership of one data partition.
A DHT is a structured peer-to-peer overlay adding consistent-hashing key routing.
A DHT partitions the key space across nodes via consistent hashing, i.e. hash-based sharding with routing.
Dynamo places keys with consistent hashing (DHT) and replicates them leaderlessly across the ring.
A router consumes from an input Message Channel and republishes to output channels.
Datatype Channel is a Message Channel constrained to carry one message type.
An endpoint is the code connecting an application to a Message Channel to send/receive.
Multiple consumers share one point-to-point Message Channel so each message goes to exactly one.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf, EIP (Competing Consumers is a Message Endpoint variant)
edges.note: Each competing consumer is a Message Endpoint; the pattern scales consumption across many of them.
A hub-and-spoke broker internally routes messages to receivers using message-routing logic.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf, EIP (Broker vs Message Bus topologies)
edges.note: Centralized hub-and-spoke broker vs distributed shared message bus are competing integration topologies.
Applications attach to the broker through message endpoints that encapsulate send/receive.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf, EIP, Canonical Data Model / Message Broker
edges.note: A hub-and-spoke broker translates between application formats via a shared Canonical Data Model to avoid pairwise translators.
A router can split a mixed stream onto per-type Datatype Channels so receivers infer type from channel.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf, EIP (Durable Subscriber / Guaranteed Delivery)
edges.note: Durable subscription plus persistent store-and-forward together ensure no message is lost while offline.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf, EIP (Durable Subscriber on a Publish-Subscribe Channel)
edges.note: A durable subscriber persists its subscription on a publish-subscribe channel to survive disconnects.
ECST consumers use durable subscriptions so state-carrying events missed while offline are still delivered.
Outbox reliably hands a message to the broker, which then guarantees end-to-end delivery via store-and-forward.
A shared queue levels bursty load while competing consumers scale out to drain it in parallel.
Competing consumers pull from a point-to-point channel that a message broker provisions and load-balances across them.
Two patterns for cross-service queries: in-memory API composition vs a maintained CQRS view database.

edges.cite: Richardson, microservices.io (API Composition resolves Database per Service queries)
edges.note: API Composition exists to answer queries that span the private databases created by Database per Service.
Assemble cross-service data by querying owners live (composition) vs pre-replicating it via state-carrying events.
An API gateway often implements API Composition, fetching from several services in parallel and aggregating one response.

edges.cite: Fowler CQRS; Richardson, Microservices Patterns ch.7
edges.note: Event sourcing supplies the event stream that CQRS read models subscribe to and project.
The CQRS query side is a materialized view kept current by subscribing to the owner's domain events.

edges.cite: Richardson, microservices.io (CQRS for querying with Database per Service)
edges.note: CQRS builds read replicas spanning services whose data is siloed by Database per Service.

edges.cite: Richardson, microservices.io (Database per Service vs Shared Database)
edges.note: Private-per-service data ownership vs one database shared by all services are opposing data-management choices.
Sagas keep data consistent across the separate databases that Database per Service creates.
Each service publishes events atomically with its own database updates via a transactional outbox.
ECST is event collaboration where each event carries the full changed state, not just a notification.
Event Collaboration is the component-collaboration style of an event-driven architecture.
Choreographed workflows are realized by components reacting to each other's broadcast events.

edges.cite: Kleppmann DDIA ch.9; Richardson Microservices Patterns ch.4
edges.note: Distributed consistency via blocking atomic commit (2PC) vs compensatable local transactions (Saga).
2PC realizes the transaction concept across multiple nodes as an atomic commitment protocol.
Marker messages propagate along the system's channels and channel state is recorded between markers.

edges.cite: Carbone et al., Apache Flink asynchronous barrier snapshotting
edges.note: Streaming engines checkpoint fault-tolerantly by injecting snapshot barriers into the dataflow.

edges.cite: Kopetz, Real-Time Systems (FTU composed of FCRs)
edges.note: An FTU is a group of replica-deterministic fault containment regions masking any single FCR's failure.
A triplicated FTU votes across its replicas' outputs to mask a faulty member.
TMR is the triplicated-with-majority-voting configuration of a fault-tolerant unit.
A primary/backup process pair is a duplex fail-silent fault-tolerant unit.
The backup monitors the primary via heartbeats and takes over when they stop.
Availability via a dedicated primary/backup pair vs a coordinated group of equivalent replicas.

edges.cite: Candea & Fox, Crash-Only Software (2003); microreboot work
edges.note: Crash-only components recover only by restart, escalating scope until the fault clears.
Erlang/OTP 'let it crash' supervision embodies crash-only design: kill and restart failed workers.
Health checks detect an unhealthy component so the crash-restart recovery path can be triggered.
Time/space partitioning (e.g. ARINC 653) enforces the boundary that keeps a fault inside its region.
Both bound the blast radius of a fault to an architecturally defined region.
An application-level gateway is a firewall that additionally terminates and inspects per protocol.
A DMZ is the segment formed between two firewall layers isolating public services.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice (security tactics)
edges.note: A firewall is a concrete realization of the Limit Access security tactic.
A DMZ realizes Limit Exposure by segregating externally reachable services from the internal network.
DMZ perimeters commonly use application-level proxy firewalls to inspect inbound traffic.
PDP/PEP externalizes the Authorize Actors tactic into a central decision point queried by enforcement points.
Zero Trust's core is a Policy Decision Point / Policy Enforcement Point evaluating every access request.
PDP/PEP is a distributed realization of the Authorization pattern with externalized declarative policy.

edges.cite: POSA2 concurrency patterns; Apache MPM (prefork vs per-connection)
edges.note: A pre-created worker pool vs spawning a fresh thread/process per accepted connection.
A prefork server is a master-worker structure: a parent that manages a pool of accepting workers.
Both pursue mechanical sympathy; low-latency designs drive the NIC from user space to cut kernel overhead.
Polled user-space queues for high-throughput I/O vs blocking kernel sockets serviced per connection.

edges.cite: POSA1 (Buschmann et al.), PAC vs MVC
edges.note: Two interactive-system patterns: a hierarchy of PAC agents vs a single MVC triad.
Both structure interactive UIs; PAC uses cooperating agent hierarchies, MVP a presenter-mediated triad.
An Adaptive Object Model is a reflective, metadata-driven realization of a meta-level architecture.
Both give runtime adaptability: a meta-level self-representation can be paired with a microkernel's plug-in extension mechanism.
A Remote Facade provides the coarse-grained remote interface onto a Service Layer.
A Remote Facade wraps fine-grained Domain Model objects behind a few coarse remote calls.
A Domain Object is a self-contained component encapsulating one unit of functionality behind an interface.
Distributed domain objects are made remotely accessible through Broker/proxy machinery.
HOPP puts an active object half on each side vs a client proxy forwarding all calls to a single remote object.
The private protocol that keeps HOPP halves consistent is an object-synchronizer policy.
An Object Synchronizer coordinates state updates among the replicas of a component group.
Authoritative-server netcode splits game state into client and server halves kept in sync, a HOPP structure.
Server owns the true simulation state; a client-server variant where clients predict and reconcile.
Networked-game consistency via one authoritative server vs peer-to-peer lockstep among clients.
Components publish and read common data on the bus, i.e. data-centric publish-subscribe.
A Data Bus is a data-centric message bus: a shared backbone replacing pairwise component links.
